rv.q: What’s most touching is that, by bringing O’Farrell’s story to stage, Chakrabarti and the creative team are able to respond by making Hamnet seem to live again.
This is a solid, elegant piece of storytelling that challenges the idea that genius is ever the work of one person alone.
While this staging loyally recreates O'Farrell's characters, it lacks her novel's emotional impact.
The characterisation is flimsy, the storytelling perfunctory and the performances strikingly uneven.

But in doing so ‘Hamnet’ loses both pathos and intrigue, turning it into an episodic, linear account of shamanic Stratford-upon-Avon lass Agnes (Madeleine Mantock), her romance with and marriage to overeducated local boy William (Tom Varey), and their subsequent parenthood and loss.
It is a production as wooden as Tom Piper’s set design.
Ingenious and intriguing, its performances hold the attention, but a stronger focus on its main characters would pay dividends.
It’s a delightful project with plenty of opportunities for reflection, but it largely lacks the emotive substance of the original material.
This rather disjointed production was, from a technical perspective, very sound.

But the piece, directed by Erica Whyman, essentially plays like a family saga of a conventional kind, with its warring families, wicked stepmother, squabbling siblings, marital stresses, told chronologically.
Alas, the show itself is a thumb-twiddling dud.
Instead this heartfelt play shows us that from great grief can come something uniquely beautiful.
It's perfectly serviceable though the conspicuous lack of dramatic conflict and Chakrabarti's inability to pull all the thematic threads tight leaves the play loosely hemmed around the edges.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this RSC adaptation of O'Farrell's bestseller, with many finding the stage version fails to capture the novel's emotional depth. While some praise its tender focus on Shakespeare's wife Agnes, others criticize flimsy characterization.
